title: Thomas Aquinas: Faith and Reason
objective: After this level you can explain how Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle with Christian theology and why he held that faith and reason cannot truly conflict.
summary: Aquinas built Aristotle into Christian theology, split truths about God into those reason can reach and those only revelation gives, and blamed any clash on faulty reasoning.

cards.headline: Can faith and reason ever really fight?
cards.body: In medieval universities, students of the arts learned mostly from Aristotle. One Dominican friar set out to show that philosophy done properly could never truly clash with Christian faith.

cards.headline: Aristotle, rebuilt
cards.body: Thomas Aquinas (about 1225 to 1274), a Dominican friar who taught theology in Paris, took Aristotle as his main inspiration and built something new: a systematic reworking of Aristotle’s philosophy inside Christian theology. He wrote long commentaries on Aristotle’s works, confident that progress in philosophy could only benefit the faith.

cards.headline: Two kinds of truth about God
cards.body: Aquinas split truths about God in two. Some, such as that God exists and that there is one God, reason can reach without revelation; he called these the preambles of faith. Others, such as the Trinity, only revelation can supply. Faith takes you further than reason can go, but it never contradicts what reason knows.

cards.headline: Blame the reasoning
cards.body: So what if a philosopher reaches a conclusion that contradicts the faith? Then, Aquinas wrote, “this is not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy, due to a failure of reason.” Truth can’t fight truth; when they seem to, someone has argued badly. On whether the world had a beginning, like Maimonides before him, he found that no demonstration works either way.

cards.headline: What “God is good” means
cards.body: Aquinas disagreed with Maimonides on one point. Reading “God is good” as only “God is not evil” misses what people mean, he argued: saying God lives means more than that God differs from lifeless things. For Aquinas, whatever good we find in creatures exists in God first, in a higher way than we can fully grasp.

cards.headline: Condemned in Paris
cards.body: Many of his views were fiercely controversial. In 1277, three years to the day after his death, 219 propositions were condemned in Paris, a significant number of which seemed to implicate his teachings. Franciscan critics published “corrections” of his work, and his Dominican supporters fired back.

cards.headline: Thomas Aquinas: Faith and Reason: the big picture
learned: Aquinas rebuilt Aristotle inside Christian theology
Reason reaches some truths about God; revelation the rest
A clash with faith means the reasoning failed
Paris condemned propositions tied to his teachings in 1277

questions.prompt: The truth about God that Aquinas thought only revelation, not reason, can supply is _____.

options.label: that God exists
options.rationale: He thought reason can reach that.

options.label: that there is one God
options.rationale: He thought reason can reach that.

options.label: that the world contains change
options.rationale: That isn’t one of his examples.

questions.explanation: Aquinas counted God’s existence and oneness as preambles reason can reach, but the Trinity needs revelation.

questions.prompt: According to Aquinas, what has gone wrong when a philosopher’s conclusion contradicts the faith?

options.label: Faith must give way to the philosopher’s conclusion
options.rationale: He said faith never contradicts true reasoning.

options.label: The reasoning failed: it’s an abuse of philosophy
There are two separate truths, both correct
options.rationale: He held truth can’t contradict truth.

options.label: Aristotle must be abandoned by Christian thinkers

questions.explanation: For Aquinas such a conclusion is not philosophy but an abuse of it, due to a failure of reason.

questions.prompt: Maimonides in Level 13 read “God is good” as a denial. What did Aquinas say it means instead?

options.label: Only that God is not evil, and nothing more
That God is the cause of goodness and nothing more
Nothing at all, since God can’t be described
options.rationale: He held the words do apply to God.

options.label: The good in creatures exists in God first, in a higher way

questions.explanation: Aquinas held positive words apply to God: the good in creatures pre-exists in God in a higher way than we grasp.
